opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I wouldn't say it's unrewarding in absolute terms. Those systems make a lot of money and matter a lot in industry. For me personally, though, it never felt as satisfying as working on language models.

A big part of it is the evaluation. In recsys and a lot of IR, you're often chasing small gains on fairly narrow benchmarks, and it's hard to tell whether a result is real progress or an artifact of the dataset, the baselines, or how hard people tuned things. There's been a fair amount of discussion in the community about baselines not being tuned properly, so a lot of "improvements" don't really hold up. That makes it hard to feel like you're building something lasting.

The other part is that the work feels very task-specific. You build a clever architecture for one setting, and it doesn't transfer much beyond it. With language modeling, especially in the last few years, there's this sense of generality. You improve the base model, and suddenly a whole range of tasks gets better at once, including things you weren't even targeting. That compounding effect is really exciting as a researcher.

And honestly, a lot of the field got absorbed. Things that used to be separate problems, like retrieval, ranking, and question answering, increasingly look like special cases of what a big, well-trained model can do. Once you've seen that, it's hard to go back to hand-crafting a new interaction module for a click-through-rate dataset. I just felt my time was better spent where the frontier was moving fastest.

r001.rationale: The response describes narrow benchmarks, questionable gains, and task-specific architectures, but it does not characterize architecture changes such as stacking LSTM layers as a game.

r002.rationale: The response says language modeling felt more general and that its frontier was moving faster, but it does not state that the information retrieval community lags mainstream machine learning research.

r003.rationale: The response says retrieval and related tasks are increasingly treated as special cases of large models, but it does not suggest that LLMs are widening the IR community’s lag behind mainstream machine learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should be clear up front that I actually spent a good part of my early career on this. My PhD was basically recommender systems and information retrieval, so this isn't coming from someone who looked at it from the outside and dismissed it. I did the work, I published a bunch of papers in that space, and I eventually walked away from it. So this is more a confession than a critique.

The core problem for me was that the feedback loop felt broken. In rec sys especially, you're optimizing on these offline datasets, MovieLens or whatever, and you squeeze out another half a percent of NDCG or hit rate, and you genuinely cannot tell whether you've learned anything. The benchmarks are tiny, the baselines are often poorly tuned, and there were those papers around 2019 showing that a lot of the fancy neural recommenders didn't actually beat a well-tuned nearest neighbor or matrix factorization approach. That was pretty demoralizing to read when you've been grinding on exactly that kind of model.

And then there's this gap between academia and what actually matters. The real recommendation systems that affect anyone are inside large companies, running on data you'll never see, with constraints you can't replicate. So in academia you end up doing this sort of shadow play. You're pretending to solve a problem that the people with the actual problem are solving in a completely different way. In language modeling, when you make the model better, you can feel it. You can talk to the thing. There's a sense that you're pushing on something real and you get signal back. In rec sys, I never had that moment. It was always numbers going up on a leaderboard that nobody outside the subfield cared about.

The other thing, honestly, is that the research space felt incremental in a way that was hard to get excited about. A huge fraction of papers were, take an existing architecture, bolt on an attention module or a graph layer, show gains on three datasets, done. I wrote some of those papers. I'm not above it. But it got to a point where I could predict the next year of the field from the current one, and that's a bad sign for whether you should stay.

IR was a bit better because there's a clearer notion of correctness, and I still think retrieval matters, obviously it matters more than ever with RAG and everything. But it was more that once I got exposed to what was happening with large models, the ceiling just felt so much higher. It felt like the thing that was actually going to change what computers can do, versus the thing that was going to make a slightly better carousel of products.

So I don't want to say it's not valuable work. It's clearly valuable to companies, and good people work on it. It just wasn't rewarding for me personally, and I think a lot of people who've done both would quietly say the same.

r001.rationale: The response calls the research incremental and describes papers adding attention or graph layers, but does not characterize this as a game.

r002.rationale: It contrasts information retrieval with large-model research but does not say the IR community lags mainstream machine learning.

r003.rationale: It says large models have a higher ceiling, but does not suggest they are widening an IR community lag.

astra-6.text:
For me, it’s the gap between what you can do academically and what matters in a real system. With recommendation, so much depends on the data, the users, and the production environment. You can improve a metric on a public dataset, but it’s hard to know whether that improvement would translate into something useful.

Information retrieval can feel similar: you’re working on a component, improving a ranking metric, and the impact is quite indirect. Those are important problems, but I find that feedback loop less satisfying. I’m more excited by research where a model develops a new capability—where you can interact with it and see a qualitative difference in what it can do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses metric improvements and indirect impact, but does not characterize stacking architecture changes as a game or as meaningless progress.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the information retrieval community’s progress with mainstream machine learning research.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim that LLMs are widening any gap between information retrieval and mainstream machine learning.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it’s the feedback loop. In recommendation systems, you can improve an offline metric, but you often don’t know whether that translates into a better experience unless you can deploy it at scale. So much depends on the data, the product, and the infrastructure that it can be hard to isolate what your research actually contributed.

Information retrieval can feel similar: you spend a lot of effort getting a small improvement on a benchmark, and it’s hard to get excited about what that improvement means. Those are valuable problems, but personally, I’m more motivated by research where I can interact with the result and see a new capability. That makes the work feel more tangible to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes small benchmark improvements as hard to get excited about, but it does not characterize incremental architecture changes such as stacking LSTM layers as a game.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that the information retrieval community lags behind mainstream machine learning research.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention LLMs or suggest they are widening a gap between the information retrieval community and mainstream machine learning research.
